anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model objects (tables, partitions, indexes, constraints, data types) are misaligned with workload access patterns, forcing even well-written SQL to use inherently inefficient access paths.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer, despite having reasonably fresh statistics, picks a noticeably sub-optimal execution plan because of cost-model errors, plan reuse quirks, or context-dependent decisions.

Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from a static physical design mismatch and an optimizer that frequently selects poor plans. Together they create an environment where sub-optimal plans are not only likely but also have no viable physical structures to fall back on, leading to extreme and unpredictable performance degradation.

Combined anomalous phenomena:  • Rampant full-table or full-index scans, some caused by missing or non-covering indexes and others by bad plan choices, making it difficult to attribute blame to a single layer.  • Wild plan variability between executions: one run may scan an entire unpartitioned table, another may attempt an index access that still requires many random I/Os because the index lacks needed columns.  • Sudden latency spikes after plan-cache invalidation, statistics refresh, or workload shifts, where a new but still poor plan amplifies the cost of an already inefficient physical design.  • Excessive CPU and I/O on both read and write paths—writes suffer from bloated or redundant indexes while reads suffer from mis-chosen join orders and scan methods.  • Performance only stabilizes when both an index is added/restructured AND plan guidance (hints, baselines) is applied, indicating the interplay of the two root causes.

Causal chain and interaction: Poor physical design supplies the optimizer with limited efficient choices; at the same time, plan-selection anomalies make the optimizer pick from those limited choices poorly. The absence of well-targeted or covering indexes inflates the estimated cost of index access, biasing the cost model toward full scans; conversely, an inaccurate cost model may underestimate the benefit of the few useful indexes that do exist, leaving them unused and masking the design flaw from simple index-usage reports. Plan reuse with skewed parameters can lock the system into a bad plan that is especially harmful given the table and index shortcomings. Together, the anomalies reinforce each other: inadequate structures magnify the impact of bad plans, while bad plans discourage investment in better structures by hiding or misrepresenting their benefit, leading to a feedback loop of degraded performance across both OLTP and OLAP workloads.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the timeout in seconds for attempts to acquire metadata locks.
entry.trigger_condition: A statement waits longer than lock_wait_timeout while attempting to acquire a metadata lock.
entry.workload_impact: The metadata lock acquisition fails and the statement does not proceed.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL server system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
